name: Emeka Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Emeka. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate technical documents from Danish and Norwegian into English, mostly for engineering firms that build parts for wind turbines. That means maintenance manuals, safety data sheets and the odd tender document, all full of torque values and part numbers. A couple of times a month I also interpret on video calls between a Danish supplier and a British buyer. I work at a rented desk in a shared office above a bike shop, because working at home with Ingrid marking school books at the same table didn't work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that technical text has right answers, and I like learning how a gearbox actually works. What wears me out is the terminology lists, which every client keeps differently, and the fact that I'm still slower than the senior people. I use a machine translator now and then for a first pass on the boring sections, but I check every number by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that didn't change much, and I'd be glad I hadn't panicked. At the shared office we'd joke about all the hype. I'd probably not post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd be fine for me. Wind energy is growing, the manuals keep coming, and safety documents need a person checking them. My rates are typical and I've got about four months saved, so I'd be comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my three main clients and try to specialise further, maybe in offshore safety documents. I'd take an online course in technical writing, about two hundred and fifty. I'd also use the machine draft a bit more on the dull bits, now that it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting a weather forecast that says it'll just be normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said comfortable. What does comfortable mean for you and Ingrid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we can pay rent on the flat near the canal, go to Copenhagen to see my dad's side once a year, and still save a bit. Ingrid's teaching pay is steady and mine goes up and down, but it averages out. We've talked about getting married in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would worry you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if one big client went. The turbine firm I do most work for is about half my income. If they moved their manuals to an agency, I'd have a bad six months.

say: I'd call AI a **useful tool** that didn't change much.
I'd **joke about the hype** at the shared office and not post anything.
think: **Wind energy** keeps growing, so the manuals keep coming.
With **four months saved** and typical rates, I'd be comfortable.
do: Take an online **technical writing course** for about two hundred and fifty.
Use the **machine draft** more on dull sections, now it's proven.
feel: **Calm**, like a forecast saying the weather will just be normal.
S0.quote: The turbine firm I do most work for is about half my income.
fieldNote: Calm makes sense: growing **sector**, steady partner income and decent savings.
His one risk is **client concentration**, which he names himself.
Uses AI **once proven**, true to his steady style.

steps.text: Specialise in offshore wind safety documents
Take an online technical writing course for about two hundred and fifty
Use machine drafts more on routine manual sections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say translators should get good at checking AI output, because that's where the work is going. I'd say it at the office and to other translators. I'd also say firms should keep humans on safety documents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my income drops a lot. Technical manuals are exactly the kind of checking and writing it describes, and the turbine firm would put them through software and send me only the safety parts. I'd keep some work, but maybe sixty percent of what I have now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the post-editing tools properly and offer clients a quality check service instead of full translation. I'd also ask the turbine firm if they need someone in-house for documentation, since that's steadier. I'd save more, pushing toward six months, and we'd delay the wedding a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but a lot less sure about the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Delaying the wedding. Have you and Ingrid talked about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not in those words, but we've talked about money. A wedding costs what we'd want for a house deposit, and if my income drops, the deposit matters more. Ingrid would understand, though her mother wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the in-house job like, compared to freelance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less freedom, but a salary and a pension, which I don't have now. I'd be writing and checking documentation, maybe running the AI tools for the whole firm. It's still thinking work, but I'd be closer to the engineers, which might help.

I'd say firms should keep **humans on safety documents**.
think: Manuals go through software, leaving me the **safety parts** only.
I'd keep maybe **sixty percent** of my current work.

Ask the turbine firm about an **in-house documentation** job.
Push savings toward **six months** and delay the wedding a year.
feel: **Anxious**, not panicking, but less sure of the next years.
S1.quote: A wedding costs what we'd want for a house deposit, and if my income drops, the deposit matters more.
fieldNote: Expects a real **income drop**, which moves him from calm to anxious.
Sees **in-house work** as safety: salary, pension, closeness to engineers.
Wedding delay shows the **household stakes** clearly.

steps.text: Learn post-editing tools and offer clients a quality check service
Apply for an in-house documentation job at the turbine firm
Put the wedding back a year to protect the house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a plan from government, with retraining for people whose work goes overnight. I'd keep it measured, I'm not an angry poster. At the office, I'd say we're all in the same boat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my translation work ends in 2028. Technical manuals are pure thinking work. The only thing I've got is that I understand the machines the manuals describe, and for three years after, people still have to fix turbines with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to train as a wind turbine technician, which is a hands-on job with a climbing certificate and electrical training. It's about a year's course, and the turbine firm sometimes sponsors people. I'd keep translating part-time to pay for it and save hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but there's a door. It's just a very fast door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're a translator. Would you really climb a turbine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've been up a wind turbine on a site visit, and I didn't hate it. That was last year. It's ninety metres and windy, and my legs were shaking. But it's a real job with real pay, and my knowledge of the manuals would actually help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in 2031 when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in trouble again, I suppose. But three years of good wages and a new skill is better than nothing. I'd hope there'd still be jobs supervising the robots out at sea.

I'd keep it **measured** and say we're all in the same boat.
think: My **translation work ends** in 2028; manuals are pure thinking work.
Knowing **turbines** helps, since hands-on repairs last three more years.
do: Train as a **wind turbine technician**, with climbing and electrical certificates.
Ask the turbine firm about **sponsoring** the course.
Keep translating **part-time** to fund training and save hard.
feel: **Alarmed**, but sees a door, just a very fast one.
S2.quote: I've been up a wind turbine on a site visit, and I didn't hate it.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot delay** cleverly, moving into hands-on turbine work.
Admits the move only buys **three years** before robots arrive.
His **technical knowledge** becomes a bridge rather than dead weight.

steps.text: Train as a wind turbine technician with climbing certificates
Save hard from part-time translation to fund the course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain sensibly, if firms and colleges plan it. I'd suggest the wind industry offers paths for technical translators. I'd say it on the industry forum, calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me. I'd translate for two more years while saving, then do the technician course. By 2031 I'd be a working technician with three years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save about four hundred a month for two years, then start the technician course in 2028. I'd keep the turbine firm as a client and ask about sponsorship early. We'd still get married, but small, in Ingrid's parents' garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a manageable way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ingrid is a teacher. Does she worry about her own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but she thinks a classroom of thirteen-year-olds needs a person. I'm not so sure in the AGI pictures, but I don't say that to her. We'd have two incomes for a while anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Small wedding in the garden. Is that a compromise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a compromise her mother would hate. But Ingrid likes the idea, honestly. A small wedding in my girlfriend's parents' garden means more money for a house deposit.

I'd suggest wind firms offer **paths for translators**.

By 2031 I'd be a **working technician** with three years before robots.

S3.quote: A small wedding in my girlfriend's parents' garden means more money for a house deposit.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a **staged plan**, so alarm drops to anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and it'd be a shame to waste it. I'd want colleges running courses now. I'd be fairly upbeat online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is good. I'd have a decade of translating and maybe a few years as a technician before 2036. I'd be thirty-seven and could switch again if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep translating and specialise in safety documents for five years, then do the technician course around 2031. We'd buy a small house in about three years. I'd keep saving, but not obsessively.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a bit of worry in the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said switch again. Into what?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No idea, honestly. Maybe supervising robots or running a maintenance team. I don't know what jobs will exist in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the house a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. Ingrid and I have looked at small terraced houses near her school. In this picture, buying in three years makes sense.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the technician plan barely works in two years. What would help is the wind industry sponsoring people like me into technician jobs. A clear training path would make all the difference.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I like the engineering side. I didn't expect to care about gearboxes, and that might be what saves me.

headlineQuote: I didn't expect to care about gearboxes, and that might be what saves me.
